title: What Does It Really Mean to Teach English?
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that English is not simply one subject among many but the discipline through which every other subject becomes accessible, since every field of study depends on language to be understood, argued, and taught. Writing as England debates whether the 'knowledge-rich era' is ending, she rejects the framing that knowledge and creativity are opposed, insisting instead that creativity only has material to work with once knowledge has been taught. Drawing on Gordon Baillie's research into English teachers' professional identity across career stages, she traces a generational tension between teachers who remember greater autonomy and early-career teachers more comfortable with prescription, and warns against English becoming a 'zombie discipline' that keeps literary study's appearance while losing its interpretive soul. She closes by defining English's deeper purpose: giving pupils both an inheritance of shared knowledge and the language to question and reshape it.
points: English is the subject that creates all others, since history depends on testimony and interpretation, science on precision and argument, and even maths on comprehending the problem before solving it.
Knowledge and creativity were never opposed: a pupil cannot subvert a sonnet's conventions without first knowing what a sonnet is, so knowledge gives creativity something to work with.

Baillie's interview research reveals a generational divide where experienced teachers mourn lost autonomy while early-career teachers more readily accept standardisation, yet every generation still defaults to the canon when asked what actually matters.
English risks becoming a 'zombie discipline' whenever exam technique displaces thought and pupils learn to ask how many marks something is worth before asking what it means.
The best English teaching doesn't choose between direct instruction and discovery or the canon and new voices; it treats these as mutually reinforcing rather than opposed camps.
quotes: We teach pupils to take marks on a page and turn them into voices, people and worlds. We ask them to sit beside the dying Mercutio, walk the streets of Victorian London, hear the wind on the Yorkshire moors and recognise the simmering fury beneath the politeness of a Jane Austen drawing room.

Yet, creativity does not emerge from emptiness. We make new ideas by combining, adapting and transforming what we already know. A pupil cannot play imaginatively with the conventions of a sonnet without first encountering sonnets.

Teachers resist the imposed knowledge-rich curriculum while often reproducing its assumptions. They criticise prescription but return to Shakespeare and the canon when asked what matters. They defend creativity while invoking a relatively traditional conception of literary culture.

Baillie warns that English risks becoming a “zombie discipline”: retaining the external appearance of literary study while losing its creative and interpretative soul. That danger is real whenever examination technique displaces thought and pupils learn to ask, “How many marks is this worth?” before asking, “What does this mean?
To teach English is to give pupils both an inheritance and a means of challenging it.
